summary: A best current practice describing how to delegate reverse DNS (IN-ADDR.ARPA) for address blocks smaller than 256 addresses, which do not fall on the usual octet boundaries. It uses a naming trick so the owner of a small block can run their own reverse zone.

plainLanguage.summary: Reverse DNS turns an IP address back into a name, and the zones for that are normally cut on round numbers. This RFC shows how to carve out a smaller piece, so that a small site can manage its own names, using a set of CNAME records that point at a zone it controls.

questions: how to delegate in-addr.arpa for a small subnet
reverse dns for fewer than 256 addresses
how to delegate reverse dns for a small subnet
why use cname records in reverse dns
subtitle: Lets small address blocks run their own reverse DNS zone.

tldr.problem: Reverse DNS zones are delegated on octet boundaries, so an organization given less than a full 256-address block cannot run its own reverse zone and must depend on whoever holds the surrounding zone.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the IN-ADDR.ARPA tree with extra labels naming the first address and the prefix length, then uses CNAME records in the parent zone to point each individual address at a child zone that the organization administers.
tldr.outcome: Address space can be handed out in smaller pieces without losing the ability to delegate the reverse mapping, and the DNS lookup algorithm needs no change at all.

today: RFC 2317 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 20), and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: What the Document Sets Out to Do
sections.content:
This document describes a way to do IN-ADDR.ARPA delegation on non-octet boundaries for address spaces covering fewer than 256 addresses. The method removes one of the objections to subnetting on non-octet boundaries and, more significantly, makes it possible to assign address space in smaller chunks than 24-bit prefixes without losing the ability to delegate authority for the corresponding IN-ADDR.ARPA mappings.

The method is fully compatible with the original DNS lookup mechanisms, so there is no need to modify the lookup algorithm and no need to modify any software that performs DNS lookups. The document also discusses some operational considerations, to give guidance in implementing the method.
sections.plainLanguage: The trick works with ordinary DNS lookups. No resolver or server has to be changed, which is what makes it practical to deploy.

sections.title: Why Reverse Delegation Blocks Small Assignments
sections.content:
With the spread of classless routing technology it became feasible to assign address space on non-octet boundaries. For a very small organization with only a few hosts, assigning a full 24-bit prefix, what was traditionally called a class C network number, often leads to inefficient use of address space.

One problem encountered when assigning a longer prefix, meaning less address space, is that it seems impossible for such an organization to maintain its own reverse zone autonomously. By using the reverse delegation method described in the RFC, the most important objection to assigning longer prefixes to unrelated organizations can be removed.

The example used assumes address space assigned to three parties: 192.0.2.0/25 to organization A, 192.0.2.128/26 to organization B, and 192.0.2.192/26 to organization C. In the classical approach this would lead to a single zone under 2.0.192.in-addr.arpa holding the PTR records for all three organizations. The administration of that zone is problematic, because authority for it can only be delegated once, which usually translates into the zone being administered by one organization. The other organizations whose addresses appear in the zone would have to depend on that organization for their address to name translation.
sections.plainLanguage: Hand out less than a full 256-address block and the reverse names for it end up in somebody else's zone, where you cannot change them yourself.

sections.title: The CNAME Trick
sections.content:
Since a single zone can only be delegated once, more delegation points are needed. These are introduced by extending the IN-ADDR.ARPA tree downwards, using the first address, or the first address together with the network mask length, as the first component in the name for the zones.

In the example, the parent zone holds a delegation for 0/25 with the name servers of organization A, and separate delegations for 128/26 and 192/26 with the name servers of organizations B and C. Each individual address in the parent zone then has a CNAME record pointing into the corresponding child zone, so that the address 1 becomes a CNAME for 1.0/25.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa, the address 129 becomes a CNAME for 129.128/26.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa, and the address 193 becomes a CNAME for 193.192/26.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa. The child zones then hold the PTR records that each organization maintains for itself.

Each size-256 chunk split up this way needs close to 256 CNAME records installed in the parent zone. Some people may view this as ugly, and the RFC does not argue the point. It is, however, quite easy to generate the CNAME records in the parent zone once and for all, automatically, if the way the address space is partitioned is known.

The advantage over the other approaches to this problem is that no already-deployed software has to be modified. In particular, the DNS lookup mechanism does not have to change to accommodate the splitting of responsibility on non-dot boundaries, and the technique had already been in use for several years in many installations, apparently with no ill effects.

A record such as a CNAME from 129 to 129.128/26.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa can conveniently be abbreviated to 129 CNAME 129.128/26. Some DNS implementations are not kind to special characters in domain names, such as the slash used in these examples. RFC 2181 makes clear that these are legal, though some might feel unsightly, and because these are not host names the host name restrictions do not apply. Modern clients and servers have an option to act in the liberal and correct fashion. The examples use the slash because it was felt to be more visible, and the RFC advises not copying them exactly, for example by substituting a more conservative character such as a hyphen.
sections.plainLanguage: The parent zone keeps the addresses but replaces each name record with a pointer. The real names live in a smaller zone that the organization owns, and the lookup machinery follows the pointer as usual.

sections.title: Other Ways to Name the Child Zones
sections.content:
As a result of this method, the location of the zone containing the actual PTR records is no longer predefined, which gives flexibility.

An alternative to using the first address, or the first address and the network mask length, to name the new zones is to use some other, non-numeric name. It is then possible to point outside the IN-ADDR.ARPA tree entirely. This alternative would be needed if two organizations shared the same physical subnet and corresponding address space, with no neat alignment of the addresses, but still wanted to administer their own IN-ADDR.ARPA mappings.

The example points out of the tree entirely: in the zone 2.0.192.in-addr.arpa, the address 1 has a CNAME to 1.A.domain. and the address 129 has a CNAME to 129.B.domain. The zone A.domain. then holds both the forward records, with host1 having an A record for 192.0.2.1, and the reverse PTR records, with 1 pointing at host1. In this way the name to address and the pointed-to address to name mapping data can end up in the same zone file, which some may see as a bonus, since no separate set of secondaries for the reverse zone is required. The traversal via the IN-ADDR.ARPA tree is still done, so the CNAME records inserted there need to point in the right direction for this to work.
sections.plainLanguage: The child zone does not have to live under the reverse tree at all. It can sit anywhere in DNS, even in the same file as the forward records, as long as the pointers point the right way.

sections.title: Running It in Practice
sections.content:
The technique is intended for delegating address spaces covering fewer than 256 addresses. For larger blocks the traditional methods of multiple delegations can be used instead.

Some older versions of name server software make no effort to find and return the pointed-to name in CNAME records if that name is not already known locally as cached or authoritative data, which can confuse resolvers because only the CNAME record is returned in the response. To avoid this problem, the RFC recommends that the authoritative name servers for the delegating zone, the one containing all the CNAME records, all run as slave name servers for the child zones delegated and pointed into via the CNAME records.

Another operational issue is that CNAME referrals cannot be provided twice for the same address space. A /25 prefix cannot be allocated to one organisation and run this way, and then be subnetted by that organisation into longer prefixes with the same technique applied again to give each subnet control of its own number space, because that would result in a CNAME record pointing at a CNAME record, which may be less robust overall.

The RFC also records that some old beta releases of the popular DNS name server implementation BIND 4.9.3 had a bug that caused problems when a CNAME record was encountered during a reverse lookup. The beta releases involved have since been obsoleted and the issue resolved in the released code, though some software manufacturers included the defective beta code in their products, and patches were available or planned in the few known cases.
sections.plainLanguage: A few practical points: make the parent servers also serve the child zones, do not nest the trick inside itself, and be aware of an old name server bug from the 1990s.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
With this scheme, the leaf sites need to rely on one more site running their DNS name service correctly than they would if they had a /24 allocation of their own. This may add an extra component that has to work for reliable name resolution.

Other than that, the authors are not aware of any additional security issues introduced by the mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The one cost is another server that has to behave correctly for names to resolve, since the reverse lookup now passes through the parent zone on its way to the child zone.

data.code:
$ORIGIN 2.0.192.in-addr.arpa.
;  <<0-127>> /25
0/25            NS      ns.A.domain.
0/25            NS      some.other.name.server.
1               CNAME   1.0/25.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa.
2               CNAME   2.0/25.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa.
;  <<128-191>> /26
128/26          NS      ns.B.domain.
129             CNAME   129.128/26.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa.

$ORIGIN 0/25.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa.
@       IN      SOA     ns.A.domain. hostmaster.A.domain. (...)
1               PTR     host1.A.domain.
2               PTR     host2.A.domain.
